summary:
Anguilla is a British Overseas Territory and the law that governs a visitor is local law; United Kingdom legislation reaches the island only where an Order in Council extends it, so no United Kingdom-level anti-discrimination floor applies of its own force.

Private consensual same-sex conduct was decriminalised by order of the Privy Council on 5 January 2001, in a decision that also covered the Cayman Islands, the British Virgin Islands, Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos Islands. The order was issued unilaterally after the local legislatures refused to repeal their statutes, and religious leaders protested the decision. Anguilla had never carried the prohibition in exactly the same statutory form as those other territories.

Anguillian law provides no protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The Constitution's anti-discrimination clause reaches race, political opinions, colour, creed, sex and place of origin, so gender identity sits outside the protected categories and a trans visitor has no statutory non-discrimination footing in local law.

The age of consent is 18 for same-sex conduct and 16 for different-sex conduct. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship therefore carries legal exposure that a different-sex couple does not face.

The Marriage Act defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman as husband and wife. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal, and Anguilla is among the British overseas territories that have not legislated for civil partnerships. A commercial destination-wedding service marketing ceremonies on the island states that same-sex marriage is not recognised under Anguillan law, so a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has access only to a symbolic, non-legal ceremony. Non-legal ceremonies of same-sex couples have taken place there.

Public LGBT life is highly constrained. A subdued and subtle climate of homophobia has pushed local LGBT people toward secrecy. The island has no pride events, gay organisations, venues, bars or clubs and no community infrastructure, which the source attributes to a population of about 15,000. The only recorded public event is a small protest on 17 May 2011 in The Valley marking the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia.

Visiting same-sex couples have described the island as gay-friendly and reported that nobody was discriminatory in any way, though the same source cautions that the position of local people may differ. A 2023 first-person account by a queer family found same-sex conduct legal under the British order but the scene muted rather than openly visible, an outcome that account attributes to decriminalisation imposed from outside rather than to local initiative.
tangentialFactors:
The 2001 decriminalisation came from the Privy Council rather than from Anguilla's own legislature, and it covered five territories at once. Anguilla's position on civil partnerships places it alongside other British overseas territories that have not legislated for them, so the absence of partnership recognition is a regional pattern among the territories rather than an Anguilla-only measure.

Anguilla is a 35-square-mile island about 100 miles east of the British Virgin Islands. The 2012 country report and the 2023 travel account both tie the absence of any LGBT venue, organisation or pride event to that small scale at least as much as to enforcement or legal prohibition.

Accounts of the island written for visitors describe a relaxed reception for visiting same-sex couples while the material on residents describes secrecy and a subdued climate of homophobia. The two bodies of evidence describe different populations, and the visitor material was produced by couples on holiday rather than by residents.

outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory sets out Anguilla's rules on gender markers on identity documents, on entry or immigration screening, or on access to sex-segregated facilities. Those questions are unresolved here.

No trans-specific violence data and no hate-crime enforcement data for Anguilla were identified, and the inventory contains no general homicide denominator for the island, so no risk magnitude for anti-trans violence can be stated.

Sources give different years for decriminalisation: the 2023 travel account states 2000, while the Privy Council order is dated 5 January 2001 and the encyclopaedic coverage gives 2001. The 2001 date is the documented one.

Whether any Order in Council has extended United Kingdom anti-discrimination legislation to Anguilla is not established in the inventory. The sources identify the mechanism but name no such order.

The favourable accounts of how visiting same-sex couples were treated describe a different population from the residents covered by the material on secrecy and lack of protection, and the sources themselves caution that local conditions may differ from the visitor experience. No source reports how a visibly trans visitor, as distinct from a same-sex couple, was received.
